section_summary: This section follows disputes over blocked Japanese balances and the convertibility of yen, including a Bolivian firm's claim and requests from American businesses. It also records British banks' request to accept yen accounts, Japan's new export exchange arrangements, and debate over sterling devaluation and sterling-funded oil purchases. The section ends with a draft of Japan's Foreign Exchange and Foreign Trade Control Law, which continues beyond page 506.

subfiles.title: Bolivian legal opinion on recovery of a Japanese credit
subfiles.about: Recommends official support for recovering a Bolivian firm's credit from the Standard Braid and Produce Company of Japan.
subfiles.summary: Recommends pursuing the $25,351.38 claim through Bolivia's embassy and the Far Eastern Commission.

subfiles.title: Draft acknowledgment of the Bolivian Embassy's claim
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the claim and explains why payment in non-Japanese currency is presently unavailable.
subfiles.summary: The Department says it has asked its representatives in Japan to investigate, but occupation controls block prewar credits and Japan lacks transferable foreign exchange.

subfiles.title: Draft note to the Bolivian ambassador
subfiles.about: Responds to Bolivia's request concerning Gumucio y Compañía's claimed Japanese credit.
subfiles.summary: Promises to seek information in Japan while warning that occupation controls and Japan's lack of foreign exchange prevent the requested transfer.

subfiles.title: Instruction to investigate the Bolivian credit
subfiles.to: Acting U.S. Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Requests an investigation of the Bolivian credit and any enemy interest in it.
subfiles.summary: Forwards Bolivia's note and asks for the credit's status and possible enemy ownership.

subfiles.title: Earlier draft instruction on the Bolivian credit
subfiles.about: Requests information on the same Bolivian claim and possible enemy interest.
subfiles.summary: Draft transmits supporting papers and requests investigation of the credit and its ownership.

subfiles.title: British banks in Japan
subfiles.about: Argues that British banks in Japan should again be allowed to accept yen accounts.
subfiles.summary: The embassy says yen accounts would help finance Japanese exports and sterling-area trade. It argues that the existing restriction discriminates against foreign traders and conflicts with occupation trade policy.

subfiles.title: Reply concerning British banks' yen facilities
subfiles.about: Responds to Britain's proposal to expand the services of British banks in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Department defends the existing licenses as nondiscriminatory and notes the extensive services foreign banks already provide. It favors discussions aimed at more normal banking arrangements, alongside renewed overseas relationships for Japanese banks and eventual Bank of Japan representation in New York and London. Foreign banks operating more broadly in Japan would be subject to Japanese banking, exchange, and tax laws.

subfiles.title: Foreign exchange rules for trade representatives in Japan
subfiles.about: Explains Japanese restrictions on foreign currency, trade representatives' funds, and export payments.
subfiles.summary: Explains conversion and deposit rules, permitted spending, and the nonconvertibility of yen profits.

subfiles.title: Northwest Airlines cover letter on Japanese cargo revenue
subfiles.from: Northwest Airlines Director of Cargo Traffic
subfiles.about: Sends a report linking declining cargo revenue to Japan's new single exchange rate.
subfiles.summary: Forwards the Japan manager's report on May cargo losses following the April 25 exchange-rate change.

subfiles.title: Past and present of Japan's export trade
subfiles.about: Reviews Japan's postwar export recovery and the effects of the ¥360-per-dollar exchange rate.
subfiles.summary: The report traces postwar export obstacles, the varied earlier conversion rates, and the growth of air cargo shipments. It weighs the administrative benefits of the April 1949 single rate against higher costs and losses for exporters, particularly smaller manufacturers. It surveys export markets and prospects and includes a table comparing 1947 and 1948 exports.

subfiles.title: Authorization to cash travelers' checks in Japan
subfiles.about: Reports new agencies authorized to exchange dollar and sterling travelers' checks for yen.
subfiles.summary: Relays a SCAP announcement extending travelers' check exchange to 130 agencies across Japan.

subfiles.title: File notation
subfiles.about: Contains a file reference and otherwise illegible notation.
subfiles.summary: File reference and brief illegible notation.

subfiles.title: Partial retention of foreign exchange by Japanese exporters
subfiles.about: Transmits SCAP's plan allowing exporters to retain portions of foreign exchange proceeds.
subfiles.summary: Explains the proposed 3, 6, and 10 percent retention rates by commodity category and permitted uses, including travel, agents, promotion, imports, and technical services. The program applies to exports shipped from June 25.

subfiles.title: SCAPIN 2020: Purchase of Foreign Exchange Credits for the Purpose of Stimulating Exports
subfiles.doc_type: enclosed SCAP memorandum and commodity schedules
subfiles.from: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Directs the creation of a controlled system for Japanese exporters to buy foreign exchange credits.
subfiles.summary: SCAP directs Japan to submit implementing plans and sets export-credit retention rates of 3, 6, or 10 percent by commodity. It limits eligible transactions, approved uses, transfer of purchase rights, and travel supported by the credits. Three detailed schedules assign products to the rate categories.

subfiles.title: Implementation of foreign exchange retention plan
subfiles.about: Reports implementation of the exporter foreign exchange retention plan.
subfiles.summary: Reports that the plan covers exports shipped from June 25 and implementing rules took effect July 15.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about converting newspaper yen balances
subfiles.about: Asks whether the North American Newspaper Alliance can convert its accumulated yen into dollars.
subfiles.summary: Requests advice on converting the alliance's Japanese yen receipts into U.S. dollars.

subfiles.title: Reply on newspaper yen balances
subfiles.about: Explains limits on yen conversion and suggests an Army inquiry about news-material payments.
subfiles.summary: Says yen is generally nonconvertible and directs Agnelli to Robert West for possible compensation arrangements.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment from North American Newspaper Alliance
subfiles.about: Acknowledges advice about the alliance's yen balance.
subfiles.summary: Thanks McDiarmid for referring the yen-balance question to Robert West.

subfiles.title: Effects of sterling devaluation on Japanese trade
subfiles.about: Assesses how sterling devaluation may affect Japan's exports, procurement, and yen policy.
subfiles.summary: Discusses uncertain effects on Japanese trade with the sterling area, including cotton textiles and procurement. It reports press opposition to immediate yen devaluation and expectations that producers should lower costs.

subfiles.title: Senator Downey forwards complaint about sterling-only oil bids
subfiles.about: Requests comment on Japan's sterling-only bids and their effect on American oil sellers.
subfiles.summary: Forwards an oil exporter's complaint and asks for advice on future sterling-only bids.

subfiles.title: American Petroleum Export Company complaint
subfiles.about: Objects to Japanese crude-oil and asphalt tenders payable only in blocked sterling.
subfiles.summary: The company says sterling-only payment excludes American producers from bids for four million barrels of crude oil and 18,000 metric tons of asphalt, despite U.S. support for Japan.

subfiles.title: Interim reply to Senator Downey
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Downey's inquiry about Japan's sterling-only oil bids.
subfiles.summary: Says the Department is examining the issue and will send a further reply.

subfiles.title: Substantive reply on Japan's sterling-funded oil imports
subfiles.about: Explains why Japan purchases some oil with sterling despite the effect on U.S. bidders.
subfiles.summary: The Department argues that spending sterling in non-dollar markets helps Japan sell exports there and reduces the U.S. taxpayer's support burden. It notes planned purchases of oil from U.S. sources as well.

subfiles.title: Draft reply on sterling-funded oil imports
subfiles.about: Sets out an earlier version of the Department's explanation of sterling oil purchases.
subfiles.summary: Draft says sterling purchases help balance Japan's non-dollar trade and reduce U.S. support costs.

subfiles.title: Representative Boggs forwards yen-devaluation inquiry
subfiles.about: Requests a report on a constituent's concern about possible yen devaluation.
subfiles.summary: Forwards Arthur Meyer's letter and requests information on possible yen devaluation.

subfiles.title: United China and Glass Company inquiry
subfiles.about: Seeks reliable information about reports that the Japanese yen may be devalued.
subfiles.summary: Meyer says devaluation would affect the company and asks Boggs for definite information.

subfiles.title: Reply to Representative Boggs on yen devaluation
subfiles.about: Provides MacArthur's statement that no yen devaluation is contemplated.
subfiles.summary: Refers Boggs to MacArthur's October 15 announcement and encloses the press statement.

subfiles.title: Statement on the yen exchange rate
subfiles.about: Announces that no devaluation of the Japanese yen is contemplated.
subfiles.summary: Says studies found no basis for changing the yen-dollar rate; export prices should adjust through other measures.

subfiles.title: London report on sterling-area procurement for Japan
subfiles.about: Reports on sterling-area purchasing plans for Japan; much of the telegram is illegible.
subfiles.summary: Discusses sterling-area purchases for Japan and a reported procurement total; details are obscured by OCR.

subfiles.title: Investigation of Gumucio y Compañía's claim
subfiles.from: Acting U.S. Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Reports findings on the Bolivian claim and asks whether German enemy-property law applies.
subfiles.summary: The claimed credit had partly been invested in Japanese shares, with the remainder still held by Standard Braid and Produce. SCAP retained the property while examining German interests in both the original creditor and its successor. The despatch cites evidence that the transfer to Gumucio may have concealed continued German ownership and requests the Department's legal opinion.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about dollar payment for consulting services
subfiles.about: Asks how Japanese chemical manufacturers can obtain dollars to pay for his engineering advice.
subfiles.summary: Seeks a way for Japanese clients to establish U.S. dollar credit for consulting services.

subfiles.title: Reply to Dr. Benner on consulting payments
subfiles.about: Explains that Japanese clients must arrange dollar payment under the new exchange-control framework.
subfiles.summary: Suggests the manufacturers arrange a letter of credit or obtain dollars through Japanese exchange authorities.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of final draft Foreign Exchange and Foreign Trade Control Law
subfiles.from: Acting U.S. Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Transmits the final draft of Japan's Foreign Exchange and Foreign Trade Control Law.
subfiles.summary: Sends the draft law and requests prompt distribution to the Department of Commerce.

subfiles.title: Final draft Foreign Exchange and Foreign Trade Control Law
subfiles.from: Japanese Government and SCAP Economic and Scientific Section
subfiles.about: Sets out proposed controls over exchange, trade, foreign payments, securities, and property transactions.
subfiles.summary: The draft states its economic purposes, defines residents and assets, and provides for a unitary exchange rate and authorized foreign exchange banks and money changers. It establishes budgeting and concentration of foreign exchange and precious metals. The pages here begin restrictions on payments, claims, securities, and immovable property; the draft continues beyond page 506.
